Computer Science Orientation, Raspberry Pi + Sense HAT

Lab 6: A Raspberry Pi

You’ll be using a tiny computer called a Raspberry Pi. Attached to the top of it is a Sense HAT: a board with a square grid of colored lights (the LED matrix) and sensors that can feel temperature, air pressure, humidity, and movement.

  • Make the Pi say “Hello world” with its lights, then show a sensor reading
  • Play a Flappy Bird game that you control by blowing on the Pi
  • Use an AI assistant to change the game so you control it by moving the Pi
  • Answer 3 short questions

A preview of the game you’ll run in Part 3.

  1. 1. Connect to the Pi
  2. 2. Say “Hello world”
  3. 3. Play Flappy Bird
  4. 4. Fix it with AI
  5. 5. Submit

Part 1

Set up and connect to the Raspberry Pi

What is SSH? SSH stands for Secure Shell. It lets you control another computer by typing commands from your own computer.

In this lab, you will use a laptop to connect to a Raspberry Pi. First you’ll plug everything together, then you’ll use the Pi’s number to connect to it remotely.

In front of you there should be a school-issued laptop, an Ethernet cable, and a box labeled Canakit.

Put the hardware together

  1. Open the Canakit box. Inside there is a box labeled USB-C (the power supply for the Pi), the Raspberry Pi box, and a case. Grab the power cable and the Raspberry Pi box.

  2. Connect the laptop to the school WiFi, then log in to the laptop with your school login (the beginning part of your email, and your password).

    The school laptops can be weird and sometimes won’t let you log in until they’re connected to the internet, so do the WiFi first.

  3. Open the Raspberry Pi box. There are two pieces. The Pi has the USB ports and a number on it. The Sense HAT is the one with the LED board (the white 8×8 square).

  4. Put the Sense HAT on the Pi. There are 40 prongs sticking out of the Pi. Line them up so the Sense HAT sits directly over the Pi, then press it on.

  5. Plug the Ethernet cable into both the laptop and the Raspberry Pi.

  6. Plug the power cable into the outlet, then plug it into the Pi.

  7. Wait 2 to 3 minutes for the Pi to boot up. The hardware setup is done.

Connect from the laptop

  1. Open Chrome, Edge, or any browser on the laptop.

  2. Open this webpage on the laptop by typing https://chester04.github.io/lab6/ into the browser. That way you have all the files you need on the laptop you will be using for the rest of class.

  3. Open a terminal on the laptop:

    1. Press the Windows key on your keyboard.
    2. Type PowerShell into the search bar.
    3. Click Windows PowerShell in the search results.

  4. Find the number on your Pi. It’s printed on top of the port where you plugged in the Ethernet cable. Type it here and the command below fills itself in.

    ssh csci1010@LAB[number on the pi].local

    Type or paste that command into the terminal and press Enter.

  5. The first time you connect, your laptop may ask whether you trust the Raspberry Pi. Type yes and press Enter.

  6. When it asks for a password, the password is password (I know, very secure).

    The password will not appear as you type. You won’t see letters, dots, or stars. This is normal. Type it anyway and press Enter.

  7. Check that you’re connected:

    hostname

    It should answer with the Pi’s name (it starts with “Lab”), not your laptop’s name.

You’re in. You have connected to a Raspberry Pi remotely using SSH. Keep this terminal open. You’ll use it for the rest of the lab.

Part 2

Say “Hello world” on the LED board

You will make the Pi scroll “Hello world!” across its lights, then show you the temperature, pressure, and humidity of the room.

  1. Make a folder for your work. Type this and press Enter:

    mkdir -p ~/projects

  2. Go into that folder:

    cd ~/projects

  3. Open a text editor called Nano. This is where you type code to make the Pi do what you want.

    nano hello_world.py

  4. Copy the Hello World code:

  5. Paste the code into Nano:

    1. Click inside the Nano editor.
    2. Press Ctrl + Shift + V, or right-click and choose Paste if that option is there.
    3. Check that the code appears in the editor.

    Don’t press plain Ctrl + V. In Nano that shortcut can do something different depending on your terminal.

  6. Save the code so you can run it:

    1. Press Ctrl + O (the letter O, not zero).
    2. Nano shows the filename at the bottom. It should say hello_world.py.
    3. Press Enter to confirm the filename.
    4. Press Ctrl + X to exit Nano.

  7. Now the fun part. Run it:

    python3 hello_world.py

    What do you see?

Want to customize it? Open the file again with nano hello_world.py. Change the words inside the quotation marks, or change [0, 255, 0] to [255, 0, 0] for red or [0, 0, 255] for blue. Save, then run it again with python3 hello_world.py.

Part 3

Play Flappy Bird, controlled by your breath

Now you will create another Python file. This time it’s a game.

How to play

  • The yellow light is your bird. The green lights are pipes that scroll in from the right, each with a gap you need to fly through.
  • Blow on the Sense HAT from 1 or 2 inches away. The bird goes up while you blow and sinks when you stop.
  • There is no game over. If you hit a pipe the bird turns red until you get out.
  • To stop the game, click in the terminal and press Ctrl + C.

  1. Open a new file in Nano:

    nano flappy_bird.py

  2. Copy the complete Flappy Bird code:

  3. Go back to the terminal and paste it into Nano, the same way as before (Ctrl + Shift + V).

  4. Save and exit, the same way as before (Ctrl + O, Enter, Ctrl + X).

  5. Now the more fun part. Run the game:

    python3 flappy_bird.py

What did you notice? Was there a delay between blowing and the bird moving? The humidity sensor takes time to detect the moisture in your breath.

In Part 4, you will use an AI assistant to change the game so you control the bird by tilting the Raspberry Pi instead.

Part 4

Fix it with AI (vibe coding)

You will ask an AI to change the game so it uses the Pi’s accelerometer instead of the humidity sensor. An accelerometer is a tiny sensor that feels movement, like the one in your phone that rotates the screen when you turn it.

The goal: the bird goes up and down when you move the Pi.

You don’t need to understand every line of Python. You need to explain what you want, test the result, and ask the AI to fix anything that doesn’t work. The point is to see how cool a Raspberry Pi is, how strong generative AI can be (and where it’s weak), and how to prompt these models well.

  1. Open an AI assistant in a new browser tab on your laptop.

  2. Write your prompt in your own words. The boxes below follow the Prompt 1 format, and the game code gets attached to the end for you.

    Prompt 1: ask for the change

    The full flappy_bird.py code is added to the end automatically.

  3. Paste the prompt into the AI assistant and send it. Read its explanation, then copy the complete code from its answer.

  4. Back in the terminal, make a new file for the AI’s version:

    nano flappy_bird_accl.py

    Paste the AI’s code in, then save and exit.

  5. Run it!

    python3 flappy_bird_accl.py

  6. Move the Pi and see what happens.

    Move it gently. It is still plugged in, so don’t yank the cables. Hold it by the edges instead of pressing on the LED board.

    Is it working as expected?

    • Does tilting the Pi move the bird?
    • Does the bird move in the direction you expected?
    • Is the bird too sensitive, or do you have to tilt the Pi too far?
    • Does the game still behave like Flappy Bird?

  7. If something doesn’t work or feels off, tell the AI and ask it to fix it. Then paste, save, and run the new code again. Repeat until you’re happy with it.

    Prompt 2: if something goes wrong or feels off

    Thanks! I ran the code and (your words). Can you fix that? Please give me the complete updated code again.

AI isn’t perfect. If the first try doesn’t work, that’s normal. Vibe coding goes in rounds: describe what you want, test the code, notice what needs improving, and ask for changes. You don’t have to get everything right on the first try.
